videos.title: Hot staging: how Starship splits in two
videos.intro: About two and a half minutes after liftoff, Super Heavy shuts down most of its engines and the ship lights its own while the two are still joined. Then they part, and the booster flips round to fly home. The chart shows why a rocket keeps speeding up as it burns off weight, using the rocket equation.
videos.facts: Flight 15 timings from SpaceX: max-Q at T+0:58, main engine cut-off at T+2:19, hot staging at T+2:21, boostback burn from T+2:26.
videos.phone: A booster that flies home can fly again, which is what makes launches cheaper.

videos.title: How Starship releases 26 Starlink satellites
videos.intro: Starship lets its satellites out one at a time through a slot in its side, like a sweets dispenser. On Flight 15 all 26 Starlink V3 satellites left between T+35:01 and T+1:17:40, about one every 102 seconds, from an orbit about 277 km up. Each satellite then climbs to its working orbit on its own thrusters.
videos.facts: V3 satellites serve Starlink dishes, not phones. Phone service runs on separate direct-to-cell satellites.
videos.phone: Bigger batches per launch make space networks cheaper to build, including the next-generation satellites built for phones.

videos.title: Catching a Starship back from orbit
videos.intro: After about 14 orbits and 22.5 hours in space, Ship 42 fell back to Starbase sideways, flipped upright, fired its engines to brake and was caught by the tower’s arms. No Starship had been caught coming back from orbit before. The chart shows how the speed at the flip sets how hard the engines have to brake.
videos.facts: Ship 42 was caught at T+22:32 on 14 Nov 2026. The Super Heavy booster called off its own catch and was lost in the Gulf of Mexico.
videos.phone: Reusable rockets mean cheaper launches, and more satellites that can talk to phones.
